rows.question: What does a CI project key start with, and how do you store it?
rows.output:
- A CI project key always begins with the prefix **`l10p_`**.  
- Create the key on your project’s **CI keys** page; it’s shown only once.  
- Store it in your CI’s secret store (e.g., GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables) and reference it as a bearer token (`Authorization: Bearer $LATITUDE10_KEY`).  
- The platform keeps only a SHA‑256 hash of the key, so never commit the raw value. Revoke and recreate it from the same page if it ever leaks.  

Docs: https://docs.latitude10.tech/registry-api and https://docs.latitude10.tech/get-started/keys-and-tokens

rows.question: Which hosts are refused as a hosted MCP base URL?
rows.output:
- URLs that are too long → “Use a shorter URL.”  
- Anything not `https` or that can’t be parsed → “Use an https:// URL.”  
- URLs containing a user name or password → “Leave out the user name and password: store the credential instead.”  
- URLs with an explicit port → “Leave out the port: only the default https port is called.”  
- URLs with a query string or fragment → “Leave out the query and the fragment: each tool adds its own.”  
- IP addresses, single‑label names, private names, **latitude10.tech** or Cloudflare‑owned names → “Use your API’s public host name, not an IP address or a private name.”  

Private names include `localhost`, `local`, `internal`, `localdomain`, `lan`, `arpa`, `test`, `invalid`, `example`, `onion`.  

See the full list: https://docs.latitude10.tech/hosted-mcp/refused-hosts

rows.question: How do I serve my docs on my own domain?
rows.output:
- Open your project’s **Docs** panel (Overview → Docs) and add the subdomain you want (e.g. `docs.example.com`). Apex domains aren’t supported yet.  
- In your DNS provider create a **CNAME** record pointing the subdomain to `domains.latitude10.tech` (the panel shows the exact record).  
- Back in the panel click **Check now**; once the hostname and the automatically‑issued TLS certificate are active the docs are live at your domain.  

Custom domains are available on Pro + plans; the number you can add depends on your plan. See the full guide: https://docs.latitude10.tech/docs-hosting/custom-domains. If you need more help, contact jorge@latitude10.tech or use https://latitude10.tech/contact.

rows.question: Is removing a property from a JSON success response a breaking change?
rows.output:
Removing a property from a JSON success response is generally considered a breaking change — especially if that property is required or if clients rely on it being present. Even when the property is optional, its removal can still cause runtime errors for code that expects the field.

**How to handle it**

- Mark the field as **deprecated** first, keep it in the response, and give clients time to stop using it.  
- When you’re ready, remove the property in a new version of the API and use the **registry’s breaking‑change diff** to see the impact between versions.  
- Update your SDKs, docs, and any client code accordingly.

You can run the diff in the Registry here: https://latitude10.tech/platform/registry. It will flag removed properties as breaking changes so you can plan the version bump safely.

rows.question: What files does a published docs site serve for AI agents?
rows.output:
A published docs site automatically provides the following files for AI agents (see https://docs.latitude10.tech/docs-hosting/agent-files):

- **/llms.txt** – list of every page (group, title, Markdown URL, description)  
- **/llms-full.txt** – full Markdown of every page (cut for very large sites)  
- **/<page>.md** – each page as raw Markdown (also returned with `Accept: text/markdown`)  
- **/skill.md** – an agent skill describing the site; you can replace it with your own  
- **/reference.md** – the API reference in Markdown (once published)  
- **/mcp** – the docs MCP server (public, read‑only)  
- **/mcp/server-card** and **/.well-known/mcp** – MCP server card (`application/mcp‑server‑card+json`)  
- **/.well-known/ai-catalog.json** – AI Catalog pointing at the server card  

These files are generated at push and served without extra setup.

rows.question: What will the API client's proxy call?
rows.output:
The API‑client proxy (available on Pro plans and up) works like this:

- Your browser sends a JSON envelope to `/r/<workspace>/<project>/proxy`.  
- Latitude 10’s server then makes a single request to the **verified HTTPS host** you supplied:  
  • only `https` on the default port, no user‑name, no IP or custom port  
  • method `GET | POST | PUT | PATCH | DELETE | HEAD | OPTIONS`  
  • body ≤ 256 KB, no cookies, no `Origin`/`Referer`, and strips headers such as `Host`, `Forwarded`, `X‑Forwarded‑*`, `CF‑*`, `Sec‑*`, `Proxy‑*`  
  • its own `User‑Agent` naming the Latitude 10 playground  
  • no redirects, a 15‑second timeout, response size ≤ 1 MB  

The response is returned as JSON (status, headers – no `Set‑Cookie`, body as text or base64, cut flag, timing).  

Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/api-client/direct-and-proxy

rows.question: What does the readiness check look at?
rows.output:
The readiness check scores an OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 spec 0 – 100 by evaluating:

- operationIds, summaries and descriptions  
- example payloads  
- request/response schemas and error schemas  
- pagination support  
- authentication configuration  
- idempotent write operations  
- total number of tools generated  

It then lists the most important fixes. The scoring rules are open‑source (MIT).
